code_label: Need for accessible practitioner guidance
text_span: Newcomers to the ﬁeld of quantum computing who are interested in using this technology to solve optimisation problems do not have an easily accessible source of information
rationale: States the motivation for the paper as a practitioner-oriented guide.

code_label: Near-term focus on noisy devices
text_span: focusing on their near-term potential for noisy intermediate scale quantum devices.
rationale: Defines the paper’s scope around NISQ-era applicability.

code_label: Quantum advantage remains unproven
text_span: it is still unclear whether these techniques will yield quantum advantage
rationale: Explicitly states uncertainty about whether the discussed techniques will outperform classical methods.

code_label: Optimization problems are hard for classical computers
text_span: The best classical algorithms for the TSP rely on heuristics and approximation methods, which can still take a long time to reach a solution
rationale: Frames why optimization is challenging and motivates quantum approaches.

code_label: Superposition alone is insufficient
text_span: superposition alone is not enough to yield an advantage.
rationale: Clarifies a conceptual limitation in naive claims about quantum speedup.

code_label: Entanglement as a key resource but poorly understood
text_span: it is believed that this will be a key resource that enables quantum advantage.
rationale: Identifies entanglement as a hypothesized resource while acknowledging uncertainty.

code_label: Simple mappings motivate problem classes
text_span: the existence of a simple mapping is itself a good reason to examine a class of problems.
rationale: Explains why problems with direct quantum mappings are attractive candidates.

code_label: No quantum advantage established in practice
text_span: true quantum advantage has not yet been established in practice.
rationale: States a central caveat about the current state of the field.

code_label: Paper aims to set expectations
text_span: with the ultimate beneﬁt of setting clear community expectations.
rationale: Describes the paper’s practical purpose for readers.

code_label: Discrete optimization is the main focus
text_span: In this work we focus almost exclusively on discrete optimisation problems.
rationale: Defines the main problem class covered in the review.

code_label: Heuristics trade optimality for efficiency
text_span: These methods are typically able to ﬁnd solutions eﬃciently (in polynomial time) but, this comes at the cost of providing a sub-optimal solution
rationale: Summarizes the classical heuristic trade-off relevant to quantum comparisons.

code_label: Quantum algorithms are typically approximate
text_span: Quantum algorithms are therefore typically approximate in nature
rationale: States the paper’s view that exact quantum solutions to NP-hard problems are unlikely.

code_label: Max-Cut maps well to Ising problems
text_span: The Max-Cut problem can be mapped to an Ising problem which makes it a good candidate for a quantum computer.
rationale: Identifies a key mapping that supports quantum algorithm design.

code_label: Quantum annealing is hardware-specific and non-universal
text_span: The kind of problem a given analog quantum computer is able to solve is closely related to the form of the hardware itself.
locator: III. OPTIMISATION ON ANALOG QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 4
rationale: Highlights a major limitation of analog quantum devices.

code_label: Adiabatic runtime depends on the energy gap
text_span: the runtime of the computation, tf is in fact gradual enough depends on the size of the energy gap between the ground and ﬁrst excited states
locator: III. OPTIMISATION ON ANALOG QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 6
rationale: Describes the key adiabatic condition governing performance.

code_label: Small gaps may make annealing impractical
text_span: The smaller the gap, the more gradual the change has to be to guarantee adiabaticity.
locator: III. OPTIMISATION ON ANALOG QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 6
rationale: States a practical constraint on adiabatic evolution.

code_label: Stoquastic annealing may be classically easy to simulate
text_span: there is concern that stoquastic Hamiltonians are easy to simulate
locator: III. OPTIMISATION ON ANALOG QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 8
rationale: Notes skepticism about the computational hardness of current annealing models.

code_label: Gate-based computers are universal
text_span: A universal digital quantum computer can, at least in principle, be applied to solve any problem of interest.
locator: IV. OPTIMISATION ON DIGITAL QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 2
rationale: States the main advantage of the gate-based paradigm.

code_label: Measurement collapses superposition to a random bit string
text_span: if you measure the superposition, you will obtain one of the states at random.
locator: IV. OPTIMISATION ON DIGITAL QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 4
rationale: Explains why algorithm design must amplify desired outcomes.

code_label: NISQ hardware limits problem size and depth
text_span: only small problem sizes can be attempted on real hardware with algorithms that are low circuit depth.
locator: IV. OPTIMISATION ON DIGITAL QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 5
rationale: Captures the main hardware constraint shaping near-term algorithms.

code_label: Variational algorithms shift work to classical optimization
text_span: utilising classical optimisers to ﬁnd optimal parameters for quantum circuits.
locator: IV. OPTIMISATION ON DIGITAL QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 6
rationale: Describes the hybrid structure of variational quantum algorithms.

code_label: Classical parameter search can be NP-hard
text_span: the problem of ﬁnding the global minimum is an NP-hard problem.
locator: IV. OPTIMISATION ON DIGITAL QUANTUM COMPUTERS, paragraph 7
rationale: Identifies a hidden classical bottleneck in variational methods.

code_label: QAOA uses cost and mixer unitaries
text_span: A single block of the circuit corresponds to the application of the cost and mixer unitaries
locator: IV.A. Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm, paragraph 2
rationale: Summarizes the core circuit structure of QAOA.

code_label: Mixer prevents trivial dynamics
text_span: the mixer unitary is required to ensure that the dynamics of the system are non-trivial.
locator: IV.A. Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm, paragraph 3
rationale: Explains the functional role of the mixer in the algorithm.

code_label: Approximation ratio measures solution quality
text_span: The approximation ratio r is deﬁned in terms of the maximum and minimum (optimal) cost
locator: IV.A. Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm, paragraph 4
rationale: Introduces the evaluation metric used throughout the review.

code_label: QUBO grows exponentially with problem size
text_span: the number of binary vectors grows exponentially (2n) with the size n.
locator: IV.A.1. Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation, paragraph 2
rationale: Explains why QUBO is computationally difficult.

code_label: QUBO can be linearly transformed to Ising
text_span: a QUBO problem can be linearly transformed into an simple Ising problem
locator: IV.A.1. Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation, paragraph 3
rationale: Describes the mapping that enables quantum implementation.

code_label: QAOA performance evidence is mixed
text_span: there is still hope that the QAO algorithm might be able to outperform classical algorithms at higher depths than have currently been explored.
rationale: Captures the paper’s balanced assessment of QAOA evidence.

code_label: Noise and compilation reduce practical speedup
text_span: under these conditions, for a given time to solution the QAO algorithm (p=4,8) was only able to solve a graph 20 times smaller than the best classical solver.
rationale: Reports a concrete comparative result under realistic conditions.

code_label: Parameter initialization can reduce classical overhead
text_span: reduce the number of classical optimisation runs to O(poly(p)).
rationale: Describes a strategy to mitigate variational training cost.

code_label: Problem structure may determine optimal parameters
text_span: The optimal parameters were found to be dependent on the topological features of the problem’s graph rather than the speciﬁc problem instance or system size.
rationale: Highlights a structural regularity in QAOA parameter behavior.

code_label: Divide-and-conquer can reduce qubit requirements
text_span: was able to achieve an average reduction of 42% in number of qubits required
rationale: Reports a resource-saving modification to QAOA.

code_label: Noise can push states toward classically samplable regimes
text_span: the quantum state towards a maximally mixed state which corresponds to a Gibbs state with β = 0
rationale: Explains a noise-based framework for bounding quantum advantage.

code_label: Hardware tests show planar problems fare better
text_span: the planar graph problems were found to have performance that was roughly constant regardless of problem size.
rationale: Summarizes an empirical hardware result about topology-sensitive performance.

code_label: Hard constraints may be necessary but costly
text_span: the evidence we have reviewed appears to suggest that hard constraints are in fact necessary to get good quality results.
rationale: States a key trade-off between solution quality and circuit cost.

code_label: Better hardware may still not be enough
text_span: there is no guarantee that we will be able to ﬁnd good variational parameters eﬃciently as problem sizes and depths grow.
rationale: Flags a fundamental uncertainty about scaling variational methods.

code_label: Need for realistic benchmarking
text_span: there is a desperate need for thorough benchmarking of existing methods using noisy simulations and real hard-ware
rationale: Identifies a concrete research need for the field.
